title: CAT's Insurance Journey
subject: Kansas Property & Casualty Insurance

attackTime.note: A rival may challenge CAT during a lesson. The chance rises from 10% at level 1 to 90% at level 9, and a challenge can cost up to a minute of the lesson clock. The final exam has no challenges.

story: CAT was a backyard alley cat in the country, and she survived on human scraps. Every winter tested her - cold nights, empty bowls, and whatever the households left behind - and she lived through each one on scraps and stubbornness.

Other cats found her along the way, and they tested her. Not with claws: with insurance knowledge. Property and casualty rules, Kansas style - which promise answers for which loss, and what happens when the clock runs out. Losing an argument stung worse than losing a fight, so she learned the rules cold.
For a long time her only goal was survival. Then one day she saw the red car, and the goal changed. She would leave with that car. Everything after that night was practice for the road out.

Nine levels stand between the backyard and the road: twenty-seven lessons, ten questions each, a ten minute clock and sixty seconds to a question. At every stop a rival cat waits to argue with her, and when the clock runs out they may strike and steal seconds from the lesson.

At the very end waits the only challenger left: SHADOW CAT, her own shadow - everything survival taught her, turned around and looking back. One hundred fifty-six questions in one hundred fifty minutes, and no tricks at all.
Win, and the mother who drives the red car brings her home. That is how CAT becomes the cardboard box tower queen - and only after that does a small black cat named BAT come into the story at all.

levels.title: The Cold Alley
levels.tagline: Where a stray cat learns what a promise is worth.

lessons.title: Two Kinds of Promise
lessons.subtitle: How a policy decides which losses it will actually answer for.
lessons.intro: Before anything else, a property policy settles one question: which causes of loss is it promising to pay for? There are two ways to answer that, and the choice colors almost everything that follows in the journey.

teaching.heading: A contract between two parties
teaching.text: A property insurance policy is a two-party contract. The insured is the first party and the insurer is the second party. When the insured suffers a covered loss, the insurer reimburses the insured up to the limits printed on the declarations page.

teaching.heading: Named peril coverage
teaching.text: Specified coverage, also called named peril coverage, answers only for the causes of loss the policy lists. If a cause of loss is not listed, the damage it does is not covered, however sudden or surprising that damage may be.

teaching.heading: Open peril coverage
teaching.text: Special coverage, also called open peril or all risk, insures against direct physical loss to the property described. Rather than naming each cause of loss it will pay for, it names the losses it will not pay for.

scenario.title: The rain that came through the roof
scenario.text: CAT has been sleeping under a torn awning behind a corner store. Overnight the wind rips the awning loose and rain ruins a stack of cardboard boxes the store kept beneath it. The owner pulls out two policies: one that lists wind among the causes of loss it covers, and one that never mentions wind but does exclude flooding. Before CAT picks a drier spot to sleep, the owner has to work out which of the two promises actually answers for the ruined boxes.

lessons.title: The Extended List
lessons.subtitle: Basic, broad, and the added causes of loss that ride together.
lessons.intro: When a policy does name its causes of loss, there is a precise sequence of lists to keep straight. Knowing which causes sit on the basic list, which arrive through extended coverage, and which appear only on the broad list keeps a coverage question from turning into guesswork.

teaching.heading: The basic cause of loss list
teaching.text: The basic cause of loss list names eleven causes of loss: fire, including hostile or unfriendly fire and the damage it causes; lightning; internal explosion; wind, including tornado, hurricane, and straight-line wind; hail; aircraft, missiles, and spacecraft; riot and civil commotion; damage by vehicles; volcanic eruption; external explosion; and smoke from a vented heating or cooking unit.

teaching.heading: Extended coverage brings the WHARVES
teaching.text: The extended coverage endorsement added to a standard fire policy brings in Wind, Hail, Aircraft, Riot, Vehicles, Explosion, Volcanic eruption, and Smoke. A handy memory aid strings their first letters into WHARVES.

teaching.heading: The broad list adds still more
teaching.text: The broad cause of loss list keeps the same causes as the basic form and then adds vandalism and malicious mischief; weight of ice, snow, or sleet; falling objects; accidental discharge of water from an appliance or plumbing; freezing of pipes; sudden and accidental tearing apart of a heating, air conditioning, or water heater unit; and damage caused by artificially generated electricity.

scenario.title: Choosing between two dry nights
scenario.text: CAT has found two possible shelters: an open carport and a locked garden shed. A neighbor explains that one policy on the property names only the basic causes of loss while another uses the broad list. Overnight a pipe in the shed freezes and bursts, and a falling branch dents the carport roof. Before choosing which building CAT should claim, the neighbor wants to know whether freezing pipes and falling objects belong to the basic list, the extended coverage endorsement, or the broad list.

lessons.title: What the Open Form Refuses
lessons.subtitle: Exclusions, catastrophic losses, and property no form will cover.
lessons.intro: Because an open peril form pays unless the loss is excluded, the exclusions carry the real weight. There are everyday exclusions, catastrophic losses excluded on every form, and kinds of property that no basic property form will cover at all.

teaching.heading: Everyday exclusions
teaching.text: An open peril form will not answer for loss caused by wear, tear, deterioration, and defects; inherent vice and mechanical breakdown; smog, rust, or other corrosion, mold, wet rot, or dry rot; smoke from agricultural smudging or industrial operations; discharge of pollutants unless a covered peril caused the discharge; or settling, shrinking, or bulging of a building.

teaching.heading: Catastrophic losses excluded everywhere
teaching.text: Earth movement; common power failure away from the premises; water damage from flood, sewer backup, and sump pump failure; neglect or intentional acts; nuclear hazards; war; and zoning laws and ordinances are excluded on every form. Earthquake can be added by endorsement, usually with a deductible of two to ten percent of the amount of coverage, and quakes and aftershocks within 72 hours count as a single occurrence.

teaching.heading: Property that is never covered
teaching.text: A basic property form does not cover property already covered by other insurance, aircraft, vehicles licensed for road use, property in which the insured has no insurable interest, land, damage to animals, birds, fish, and rodents unless they are business inventory, patios and pavement, or an unrelated tenant's property.

scenario.title: The burst pipe and the muddy water
scenario.text: Heavy rain floods the alley behind the corner store, and muddy water seeps into the shed where CAT shelters. The shed is old, and its foundation has begun to settle and crack. The owner asks whether the open peril form on the shed will answer for the flood damage, for the settling, and for a rented scooter parked inside that is licensed for road use. CAT waits while the owner sorts out which of these losses the form pays for and which it refuses by design.

levels.title: The Warm Doorstep
levels.tagline: The porch light is on, but the fine print is on the door.

lessons.title: Conditions of the Contract
lessons.subtitle: Cancellation, deductibles, other insurance, vacancy, and coinsurance.
lessons.intro: Conditions are the fine print wrapped around the promise. They fix how long the promise runs, how either side may walk away, how two policies split one loss, and what happens when the insured carries too little coverage for the building.

teaching.heading: Time and territory
teaching.text: A covered loss has to happen while the policy period printed on the declarations page is still running. The policy territory fixes where coverage reaches, and it can stretch from the whole world down to one address depending on how the contract is written.

teaching.heading: Cancellation and nonrenewal
teaching.text: When premium goes unpaid the insurer must give at least 10 days notice; every other reason needs at least 30 days. The insurer may cancel for any reason during the first 60 days, or 90 days on a commercial policy, and after that only for reasons the policy lists. Nonrenewal calls for at least 30 days notice, 60 days on commercial. The insured, on the other hand, may cancel at any time simply by writing to the insurer.

teaching.heading: Coinsurance
teaching.text: Coinsurance, sometimes called insurance to value, asks the insured to carry a limit equal to at least 80 percent of what it would cost to rebuild the building at the time of the loss. Miss that mark and the insurer may cut the payment by the ratio of limit carried to limit required, applied to the amount of the loss.

scenario.title: Two policies and one small fire
scenario.text: The grocery store owner keeps two property policies: one that names the shed by its address, and a blanket policy that does not. A space heater fire scorches the shed; the deductible is $250. The owner also confesses the building limit is only 60 percent of what rebuilding would cost and wonders whether that is a problem. CAT watches from the windowsill while the owner works out which policy answers first, what role the deductible plays, and how running light on insurance reshapes the settlement.

lessons.title: Duties, Subrogation, and Settlement
lessons.subtitle: What each side must do after a loss, and who ends up owning the remains.
lessons.intro: Once a loss happens the policy stops being a promise and becomes a to-do list. The insured reports and protects; the insurer settles and may recover. The time limits are exact, which is exactly why these provisions show up on nearly every property exam.

teaching.heading: The insured's duties after a loss
teaching.text: The insured must call the police when a crime is involved, tell the insurer, shield the property from more damage, and deliver proof of loss within 60 days showing values, evidence and receipts. Transferring rights and duties to a new owner only counts once the insurer agrees in writing. In Kansas an insured may sue for up to five years after the loss, but not before every policy provision has been satisfied.

teaching.heading: The insurer's provisions
teaching.text: Liberalization makes any revision that widens coverage mid-term apply on its own, as long as no extra premium is owed. Subrogation obliges the insured to hand the insurer the right to recover from whoever caused the damage, letting the insurer stand in the insured's shoes. Salvage hands the insurer every right to the salvage value once it has paid for the damaged property.

teaching.heading: How losses are settled and paid
teaching.text: Buildings are normally settled at replacement cost, while contents and outdoor property are settled at actual cash value. The insurer has 30 days to pay after proof of loss is filed, after a court judgment, or after an appraisal award. Under the appraisal clause each side names an appraiser, and if the two disagree they pick a third - an umpire - whose decision binds everyone.

scenario.title: The neighbor's fallen tree
scenario.text: A neighbor's long-neglected tree topples onto the shed. The owner calls the insurer, nails boards over the hole so rain cannot do more damage, and files proof of loss. The insurer pays, then announces it will chase the neighbor for what it spent. It also informs the owner that the salvage value of the ruined roofing is now the insurer's. CAT dozes in a dry corner while the owner learns what a covered loss demands of each side.

lessons.title: Words That Decide Claims
lessons.subtitle: Definitions, valuation methods, and the mortgage clause.
lessons.intro: Most coverage fights are really definition fights. The vocabulary decides them - agreed value, direct loss, unoccupied, vacant - and two third-party conditions quietly protect a lender and an estate.

teaching.heading: Third-party conditions
teaching.text: The standard mortgage clause guards the lender's interest and lets the lender file a claim when the insured will not, and it keeps coverage alive for the lender even if the insured deliberately damages the property. The insurer must give the lender at least 10 days notice before cancellation or nonrenewal. If the insured dies, the legal representative of the estate steps into the insured's place until the estate is closed.

teaching.heading: Valuation methods
teaching.text: Actual cash value is replacement cost minus depreciation, obsolescence or deterioration. Replacement cost is what it costs today, at present labor and material prices, to repair or rebuild. Market value is the current selling or negotiated price of the building and is used to set the limit on older buildings.

teaching.heading: Definitions that move limits
teaching.text: Agreed value is a value settled and fixed when the policy is issued, and it becomes the most the policy will pay for a covered loss; if the named insured keeps agreed value in place, no coinsurance penalty is charged on partial losses. Blanket coverage puts several locations or items under one policy, while scheduled coverage lists each item on its own with a separate limit and premium.

scenario.title: The locked shed and the missing rent
scenario.text: A small local lender holds the mortgage on the shed, and the owner has agreed the shed's value with the insurer ahead of time. A windstorm peels off part of the roof, and the renter who stored tools there loses a month of use. CAT settles onto the paperwork while the owner sorts through three puzzles: what the lender is entitled to, what agreed value does to the coinsurance penalty, and whether the lost rental income is a direct loss or an indirect one.

levels.title: The Garden Path
levels.tagline: A garden stays peaceful until someone else gets hurt in it.

lessons.title: Liability Begins with Fault
lessons.subtitle: How fault is measured, who counts as a visitor, and what a court can award.
lessons.intro: Property coverage pays the insured. Liability coverage pays a stranger because of the insured. This lesson sets out the roles in that arrangement, the vocabulary that decides who was at fault, and the categories that decide what the fault is worth.

teaching.heading: Who pays whom
teaching.text: A liability claim brings together the insured, the insured's insurer, and the injured party who collects, who is called the claimant. The insurer pays whatever sums the insured becomes legally obligated to pay up to the stated limit, and it pays investigation and defense costs, attorney fees included, on top of that limit rather than out of it.

teaching.heading: What counts as negligence
teaching.text: Negligence is not doing what a reasonable person would do under the same or similar circumstances, and tort, or civil, law decides fault and the size of an award. The duty owed depends on who was present: an invitee was specifically invited, a licensee covers friends, family, and regular callers such as letter carriers and trash collectors, and a trespasser may be casual or criminal.

teaching.heading: Damages, and liability without fault
teaching.text: Actual, or compensatory, damages are split into special damages for medical bills, lost income, rehabilitation and direct expenses, and general damages for pain and suffering, loss of companionship and mental anguish. Punitive damages are meant to punish and set an example, and insurance does not pay them. Absolute liability applies with no fault at all, as with hazardous property, while strict liability holds a maker responsible for harm its product causes even if the buyer handled it carelessly.

scenario.title: The cracked loading apron
scenario.text: A courier crossing the hardware store's loading apron catches a boot on a cracked slab and goes down hard, breaking a wrist. He had been invited there to drop a pallet, and the owner had known for weeks that the slab was crumbling away. The insurer retains an attorney before anyone files a lawsuit. Watching from a shelf of paint cans, CAT hears the owner work through three puzzles: who exactly is the claimant, what the insurer pays beyond its stated limit, and how a jury would separate the hospital bills from the pain and suffering.

lessons.title: Limits and Common Provisions
lessons.subtitle: How much a liability policy pays, and how its shared clauses work.
lessons.intro: Liability forms borrow many provisions from property forms and then add a family of limits. Reading a limit correctly, and knowing that coverage applies separately to each insured without enlarging that limit, is the skill this lesson builds.

teaching.heading: Provisions carried over from property
teaching.text: The occurrence must take place during the policy period. Cancellation follows a familiar pattern: ten days notice for non-payment and thirty days for other reasons. Where other insurance exists, the policy with the most specific coverage pays first as primary, or the insurers share pro rata. Assignment needs the insurer's written approval, and subrogation transfers the right of recovery against a responsible third party.

teaching.heading: The five ways a limit is written
teaching.text: Per occurrence is the ceiling for any single event. Per person is the ceiling for any one individual. Aggregate is the ceiling for all claims combined across one policy period. Split limits give separate figures for bodily injury and property damage that cannot be borrowed from one another, while a combined single limit applies one figure to bodily injury and property damage together.

teaching.heading: Duties after a loss, and separability
teaching.text: The insured must tell the company promptly about an occurrence, a claim or a suit, forward copies of legal notices, allow the company to obtain records, cooperate, and neither pay nor assume any obligation without the insurer's consent. Bankruptcy of the insured does not release the insurer from its duties. Separation of insureds applies coverage separately to each insured but does not increase the limit for any single occurrence.

scenario.title: One afternoon, two harms
scenario.text: A visiting terrier nips a courier on the ankle, and not an hour later the same dog sends a display of paint cans crashing down. It is a single afternoon but two kinds of harm, and the store carries a policy with a per-person limit, a per-occurrence limit, and an aggregate. The owner also wonders whether the neighbor who was minding the dog counts as an insured. CAT, skilled at staying unnoticed, watches while the owner learns that one occurrence cannot be charged against the limit twice.

lessons.title: Defending a Claim
lessons.subtitle: Shared fault, accepted risk, and breaking the chain of cause.
lessons.intro: Liability basics close with the defenses that decide whether a claim survives at all. Some erase recovery entirely, some merely shrink it, and one shifts the blame to a later cause instead.

teaching.heading: Defenses that erase recovery
teaching.text: Contributory negligence is a common law defense: a person who contributes in any way to a loss is barred from recovering from another, even if the other party was mostly at fault. Assumption of risk is also a common law defense, and a plaintiff who voluntarily takes on the risk may be barred, as when an adult rides in the back of a pickup.

teaching.heading: Defenses that divide the loss
teaching.text: Comparative negligence is a statutory defense that weighs the conduct of every party to set the percentage of fault and the size of the award. The party carrying the highest percentage of fault pays that share of the other person's damages or injuries.

teaching.heading: Defenses that move the blame
teaching.text: An intervening cause frees the defendant of liability. Picture a dropped cigarette starting a fire in a dormitory, only for investigators to find that a smoke detector had failed; had the detector worked, the damage would have been slight. That failure becomes the proximate cause and relieves the student of responsibility. A statute of limitations requires suits to be brought within the time period set by law.

scenario.title: The pickup bed and the leaning fence
scenario.text: A teenager rides in the open bed of a pickup, as neighbors have done for years, and is thrown clear when the truck jounces over a rut. The driver points out that the fence he swerved around had been leaning for months. CAT, who has survived on the street by reading risk early, listens while the adjuster weighs three defenses: one that could erase the passenger's claim outright, one that divides blame by percentage, and one that pins the real cause on something later in the chain.

levels.title: The Sunny Wall
levels.tagline: A house, a wall, and a cat who knows every window.

lessons.title: Inside a Homeowners Policy
lessons.subtitle: The six coverages, the Kansas protections, and the endorsements that reshape them.
lessons.intro: A homeowners policy folds property and liability protection into a single package. Its declarations page spells out six coverages, and endorsements decide how far each of them really reaches.

teaching.heading: The six coverages
teaching.text: Coverage A is the dwelling itself, carried at replacement cost. Coverage B, other structures, rides along as an additional ten percent of A, paying replacement cost on buildings but actual cash value on other property. Coverage C, unscheduled personal property, adds fifty percent of A, settles at actual cash value, and follows the insured anywhere in the world up to one hundred percent of its limit. Coverage D, loss of use, adds thirty percent of A for indirect costs such as additional living expenses or lost rent. Section II brings Coverage E, personal liability, at one hundred thousand dollars per occurrence, and Coverage F, medical payments to others, at one thousand dollars per person up to twenty-five thousand dollars per occurrence.

teaching.heading: One package, two sections
teaching.text: A homeowners policy answers both the property and the liability exposures of an ordinary household in one contract. Kansas adds two timing protections to the fine print: an insured may sue the company for up to five years rather than the usual one, and a covered loss must be paid within thirty days rather than sixty.

teaching.heading: Endorsements that change the deal
teaching.text: Personal property replacement cost coverage lifts contents from actual cash value to replacement cost. Scheduled personal property lists valuables such as furs, jewelry, silverware, coins, fine art, and stamps at agreed value with no deductible and open peril coverage worldwide. Water backup and sump pump discharge or overflow pays up to five thousand dollars after a two hundred fifty dollar deductible. Inflation guard keeps the eighty percent coinsurance requirement in step with rising building costs, and personal injury responds to lawsuits including defamation, wrongful arrest, and wrongful eviction.

scenario.title: Reading a declarations page on the wall
scenario.text: The grocery owner's sister has inherited a modest house, and she reads its declarations page out loud while CAT stretches along the warm top of the garden wall. Coverage A shows one hundred thousand dollars, and the questions come in a rush: how much sits behind the other structures, what limit follows the unscheduled contents, could the family be paid for a hotel if the house became uninhabitable, and how much medical payments coverage is really there. Each answer moves the boundary between what the household carries and what the policy carries.

lessons.title: Who Counts as an Insured
lessons.subtitle: The named insured, the broader class of insureds, the insured location, and eligible dwellings.
lessons.intro: Many homeowners questions are really questions about membership. The policy defines who the named insured is, who else counts as an insured, what places count as the insured location, and which dwellings are simply not eligible.

teaching.heading: Named insured and insureds
teaching.text: The named insured is the person on the declarations page: you, together with your spouse if the two of you share a household. The term insured reaches further, to residents of your household who are related to you by blood, adoption, or marriage, and to anyone under twenty-one in the care of you or one of those relatives, such as a foster child or an exchange student.

teaching.heading: What counts as an insured location
teaching.text: The insured location starts with the residence premises. It also takes in the portion of other premises, structures, and grounds you use as a residence; a residence you buy during the policy period for your own use; any part of a premises you do not own where an insured is staying temporarily; vacant land you own or rent that is not farmland; and family cemetery plots or burial vaults, up to five thousand dollars.

teaching.heading: Who and what qualifies
teaching.text: The dwelling must be a one-to-four family home used mainly for residential purposes and lived in by its owner. Up to two roomers or boarders are allowed, and a tenant's own belongings are not covered. Farms and businesses fall outside the form. A small service business with no more than two employees may run inside the home, such as a barber shop or a professional office, but retail sales, manufacturing, wholesale distribution, and auto repair may not. Other structures slip out of Coverage B the moment they are used for any business purpose, although a garage rented to someone else purely for parking a car, boat, or motorcycle keeps its coverage.

scenario.title: A house with several kinds of resident
scenario.text: A narrow house near the alley holds a grandmother, her adult nephew, a foster child, and one paying boarder. The owner's cousin asks CAT to sort out who belongs to whom: do the nephew's work tools travel with the policy, is the boarder's laptop ever covered, and does the detached garage still qualify now that a neighbor pays to park there. CAT, who appears on nobody's declarations page, listens while the questions of membership and location get untangled.

lessons.title: Choosing a Homeowners Form
lessons.subtitle: HO-2, HO-3, HO-5, the renters and condo forms, and the losses that no form covers.
lessons.intro: Homeowners forms do not all insure the same causes of loss. Lined up side by side, the difference between broad named perils and special coverage becomes obvious, along with the losses that no form on the market will pay for.

teaching.heading: The form numbers
teaching.text: The HO-2 broad form applies broad named perils to coverages A, B, and C. The HO-3 special form moves coverages A and B to a special, open peril basis while leaving C on broad named perils. The HO-5 comprehensive form puts a special cause of loss on A, B, and C alike. The HO-8 modified form stays with basic named perils and adds vandalism, malicious mischief, and theft, capping personal property at one thousand dollars and settling at actual cash value or repair cost up to market value.

teaching.heading: Renters and condominium owners
teaching.text: The HO-4 contents broad form is built for tenants: it skips coverages A and B, applies broad perils to Coverage C, and devotes ten percent of C to tenants improvements, also called building additions and alterations. The HO-6 condominium unit owners form applies broad named perils to coverages A and C and needs no Coverage B. The outer shell of the building and any separate structures owned by the association are insured under the association's commercial policy, and each owner then insures their own unit with an HO-6.

teaching.heading: What no form covers
teaching.text: Every homeowners form turns down the same core list. Earth movement of any kind, including earthquake, landslide, mine subsidence, and sinkhole collapse, is out. So is water damage from surface water, which takes in flood, ground water, sewer backup, and sump pump failure. Ordinance or law is excluded, although Kansas permits ten percent of the Coverage A limit for it. Common power failure, neglect, intentional loss, and war or nuclear hazard are all excluded too. Every form still shares the same Section II personal liability coverage, and every form covers theft of personal property.

scenario.title: Four very different homes on one street
scenario.text: Four households share a single street: an old house insured on a modified form, a family home on a special form, a unit inside a condominium building, and an apartment rented by a student. A hailstorm sweeps through, a sinkhole opens two streets away, and the student's laptop vanishes from the apartment. CAT walks the fence line while the adjuster works through which form answers which loss, and which loss no form on the street will answer at all.

levels.title: The Rooftop Run
levels.tagline: Up here the wind bites and the sub-limits bite back.

lessons.title: Inside Limits and the Gaps in Coverage
lessons.subtitle: Small ceilings stacked on personal property, and what a homeowners form refuses outright.
lessons.intro: Unscheduled personal property reads as though it has no ceiling at all, yet narrow caps sit on whole categories of valuables, and a separate list names property the form will not touch. These ceilings show up on nearly every exam because they are so easy to mix up.

teaching.heading: Caps that apply to theft
teaching.text: The narrow caps work category by category. When furs, jewelry, stones or watches are stolen, misplaced or simply lost, the ceiling is one thousand five hundred dollars. Guns get twenty-five hundred dollars, and pewterware, goldware and silverware get twenty-five hundred dollars as well.

teaching.heading: Caps that apply to every peril
teaching.text: Banknotes, gold, silver and money top out at two hundred dollars when any peril is involved. One thousand five hundred dollars covers rebuilding personal records, securities, accounts, deeds, passports, evidence of debt, manuscripts, tickets, stamps, watercraft, trailers and motors. Property used mainly for business gets twenty-five hundred dollars, dropping to fifteen hundred when the property sits off the residence premises. Portable electronic equipment that can draw power from a vehicle as well as another source is capped at fifteen hundred dollars while inside or upon a motor vehicle or away from the residence premises, and media such as tapes, wires, records and disks are capped at two hundred fifty dollars.

teaching.heading: Property the form will not cover
teaching.text: Under coverages A and B, land is not covered, and that includes the ground the structures stand on. Under Coverage C, property that other insurance already covers is excluded, and the form also leaves out aircraft other than models, motor vehicles except those used to service the residence or assist the handicapped, harm to animals, birds and fish, a tenant's property when the tenant is unrelated, and business data whether it is on paper or in a computer.

scenario.title: The shoebox left upstairs
scenario.text: A tenant clears out of the upstairs flat and forgets a shoebox. It holds a gold ring, a set of antique silver spoons, a passport, a stamped coin collection, and a laptop that charges in a car as readily as at a wall outlet. Someone lifts the box from an unlocked car the following morning. CAT watches the owner sort the contents into categories and try to work out what each one is actually worth.

lessons.title: Section I Add-On Coverages
lessons.subtitle: The add-ons, the extensions, and what each one actually pays.
lessons.intro: The add-on coverages come in two shapes. An addition raises a limit, while an extension lets the insured move unused limits somewhere else. Each one carries its own figure.

teaching.heading: Additions against extensions
teaching.text: An addition raises the limit of insurance the policy provides. An extension leaves the limit alone and instead lets the insured pour unused limits from one coverage into another.

teaching.heading: The figures to know
teaching.text: Debris removal is an extension, with an extra five percent of Coverage A available once the loss plus debris removal runs past the policy limit, plus five hundred dollars per tree up to one thousand dollars total for trees brought down by wind, hail or ice, or for a neighbor's tree felled by a covered peril that damages a covered structure. Trees, shrubs and other plants are an addition of five percent of Coverage A with a five hundred dollar ceiling per item. The fire department service charge is five hundred dollars with no deductible. Property moved to protect it keeps coverage for thirty days against direct loss from any cause. Credit card, fund transfer card, forgery and counterfeit money is an extension of five hundred dollars with no deductible. Loss assessment is an addition of one thousand dollars, and landlord's furnishings is an addition of twenty-five hundred dollars on broad perils except theft.

teaching.heading: Landscaping and collapse
teaching.text: Landscaping is covered for fire or lightning, explosion, riot or civil commotion, aircraft, non-owned vehicles, vandalism and malicious mischief, and theft, but wind, hail, ice and snow are left out. Collapse is not a peril in its own right, yet coverage applies when a building under coverages A and B collapses because of a peril insured against, the weight of people or property, or hidden insect and decay damage.

scenario.title: The oak that came down
scenario.text: A windstorm splits the store's oak, which lands across the fence and leaves branches blocking the alley CAT crosses at night. Clearing the tree runs past the policy limit for the loss. The fire department bills for the call, and the owner misplaces a credit card the same week. CAT circles the wreckage while the owner stacks up five hundred dollars per tree, five percent of Coverage A, and a separate five hundred dollars for the fire department, trying to tell the additions from the extensions.

lessons.title: Section II Liability and Supplementary Payments
lessons.subtitle: Coverages E and F, defense costs, and what is paid on top of the limits.
lessons.intro: Section II turns the homeowners policy into a liability policy. It pays damages and defense, adds medical payments whether or not anyone was at fault, and then stacks supplementary payments on top of the limits.

teaching.heading: Coverage E, personal liability
teaching.text: The minimum combined single limit is one hundred thousand dollars per occurrence. Under the insuring agreement the insurer pays up to its limit for damages the insured is legally liable for and provides a defense at its own expense through counsel it chooses, even when the suit is groundless, false or fraudulent. The insurer may investigate and settle any claim it sees fit, and the duty to settle or defend ends once the limit for that occurrence has been used up.

teaching.heading: Coverage F, medical payments to others
teaching.text: The minimum limits are one thousand dollars per person and twenty-five thousand dollars in the aggregate, payable for up to three years from the date of the accident whether or not anyone was at fault. Medical expenses covers reasonable charges for medical, surgical, x-ray, dental, ambulance, hospital, professional nursing, prosthetic devices and funeral services. Coverage does not reach the insured or regular household residents, except residence employees. For everyone else it applies to a person on the insured location with an insured's permission, or off the insured location when the injury grows out of a condition on the insured location or the ways immediately adjoining, comes from an insured's activities, comes from a residence employee acting in the course of employment, or comes from an animal owned by or in the care of an insured.

teaching.heading: Supplementary payments
teaching.text: Supplementary payments are made on top of the limits of liability. They take in claim expenses such as costs the insurer incurs and costs taxed against the insured in any suit it defends, a two hundred fifty dollar premium for bail bonds, premiums on appeal bonds, interest that accrues after judgment along with prejudgment interest, and reasonable expenses the insurer asks the insured to incur, including actual lost earnings up to two hundred fifty dollars per day. Every liability contract carries these supplementary payments.

scenario.title: The bite at the garden gate
scenario.text: A child reaches through the garden gate to pet a dog and gets bitten. The family has no wish to sue, but the child needs stitches and a tetanus shot, and the bills trickle in over the next few months. The dog belongs to the household. The insurer also sends a lawyer once the family hints at a claim. CAT, who has firm views about dogs, listens while the owner untangles medical payments made regardless of fault from the defense costs paid on top of the liability limit.

levels.title: The Outer Yards
levels.tagline: Past the garden wall the policies change shape.

lessons.title: When Liability Steps Back
lessons.subtitle: The claims Sections E and F refuse, and the narrow ways back in.
lessons.intro: Liability coverage is generous on purpose, which is why it also lists its refusals so carefully. A few of those refusals carry small exceptions, and it is usually the exception - not the rule - that settles a claim.

teaching.heading: Harm that was intended
teaching.text: Sections E and F turn away bodily injury or property damage that an insured expected or meant to cause. There is one carve-out: property damage of up to one thousand dollars that results from the deliberate act of a child under thirteen is still answered. The policy also refuses vicarious liability for a minor's use of a car, an aircraft or a watercraft, because those exposures belong to auto, aviation and boat coverage. Running a business is refused too, unless the insured is under twenty-one and the work is a part-time or occasional self-employment. Supplying professional services is refused as well.

teaching.heading: Cars, boats and aircraft
teaching.text: Owning, maintaining, using, loading or unloading a motor vehicle is refused, with four exceptions: a vehicle that services the insured's residence, a vehicle that serves the handicapped, a golf cart used to play golf, and a battery-powered toy for a child under seven that cannot top five miles per hour. Watercraft are refused unless they are owned or rented boats with outboards of twenty-five horsepower or less, sailboats of twenty-six feet or less, or rented boats with inboard or inboard-outdrive engines of fifty horsepower or less. Aircraft and hovercraft are refused except for models. Damage to property the insured owns, rents or uses is refused under the care, custody and control rule.

teaching.heading: The rest of the list
teaching.text: Sections E and F also refuse lawsuits that grow out of passing on a communicable disease, out of sexual molestation, out of corporal punishment, and out of physical or mental abuse by an insured. Claims tied to the use, sale, manufacture, delivery, transfer or possession of a controlled substance are refused as well.

scenario.title: The pond, the golf cart, and the boy on the bicycle
scenario.text: One afternoon at the store owner's household gathers a neighbour's pond, a golf cart used out on the course, and a twelve-year-old with a good arm and a rock. The insurer has to sort which of the day's claims Sections E and F will answer and which they will turn away. CAT, who once rode out a winter in a boat shed, pays close attention to the horsepower ceilings and to the child's age, because those small numbers are what decide the whole thing.

lessons.title: Farm and Dwelling Programs
lessons.subtitle: The farmowners spinoff and a dwelling policy that is only property.
lessons.intro: Not every dwelling belongs in the homeowners program. There is a farmowners policy built off the homeowners forms, and a dwelling policy that is a pure property contract with liability sold only as an option.

teaching.heading: Farmowners in outline
teaching.text: A farmowners policy can be sold on its own or inside a commercial package, and it draws on four farm coverage forms: the farm property form, whose causes of loss may be basic, broad or special; the mobile agricultural machinery and equipment form; the livestock coverage form; and the farm liability coverage form. Property coverages A through D match the homeowners policies. The livestock form answers for animals on the premises that wander into a neighbour's field and are hurt or cause damage, and it turns away animals in transit, animals at sale barns and stockyards, breed-specific diseases, and damage from vehicles - though it does answer for strangulation, electrocution and drowning. Custom combining is picked up under personal liability when the yearly receipts from it stay under two thousand dollars.

teaching.heading: What the dwelling policy is for
teaching.text: The dwelling policy is a property policy, not a package policy. It is built mainly for dwellings rented out to others, and it also fits owner-occupied homes that cannot qualify for a homeowners policy because the property is too old or too small. It will accept a single-family dwelling and up to four units, with as many as five boarders in one structure. Farms and businesses are out, apart from an incidental service business with two or fewer employees. Every coverage carries a two hundred fifty dollar standard deductible. Personal liability can be added as an option, and it then matches Section II of the homeowners policy.

teaching.heading: Three dwelling forms
teaching.text: The DP-1 basic form values the dwelling at actual cash value with no coinsurance, extends ten percent for other structures, and offers no additional living expenses. The DP-2 broad form and the DP-3 special form value the dwelling at replacement cost with an eighty percent coinsurance requirement and add other structures, fair rental value, additional living expenses and theft of building parts. The vacancy period on the dwelling forms runs sixty days, and every dwelling policy leaves theft of personal property out unless the broad theft endorsement is attached.

scenario.title: The rented farmhouse and the cramped cottage
scenario.text: Out past the yards, a rented farmhouse needs coverage, and a small old cottage is too cramped to fit the homeowners program at all. The same owner keeps a few cows that now and then wander into a neighbour's field and do damage. CAT, who regards a barn as a five-star hotel, listens while the agent works out which policy answers for the wandering livestock, which form demands coinsurance, and which one never offers additional living expenses in the first place.

lessons.title: Homes on Wheels
lessons.subtitle: MH-1, MH-2, MH-3 and what a home must do to qualify.
lessons.intro: The mobile homeowners program is short and strict: three forms, one settlement basis, and a set of conditions the home has to meet before the policy applies at all.

teaching.heading: Three forms, one basis
teaching.text: The mobile homeowners program offers the MH-1, MH-2 and MH-3 forms, and every one of them settles losses on an actual cash value basis only. Camping trailers and motor homes are outside the program entirely.

teaching.heading: Permanently placed
teaching.text: For the policy to apply, the mobile home must be permanently located, skirted, tied down, and have its wheels taken off. The policy does not answer for the home while it is being transported or moved to a new location.

teaching.heading: When it does not qualify
teaching.text: A mobile home that cannot qualify for an MH policy can still be written on a DP-1 dwelling policy. A handy memory aid for the form numbers is worth remembering here: an even number marks broad coverage and an odd number marks special coverage, apart from the high 8 and the low 1.

scenario.title: The home with wheels
scenario.text: Behind the outer yards sits a mobile home whose owners have pulled the wheels, tied it down and skirted the base. Across the road a family is still using their camper as a summer cottage, and they are surprised when the agent explains that the mobile homeowners program will not touch it. CAT, who has slept in worse boxes than either one, waits to hear which settlement basis fits the home with wheels - and what a DP-1 would do for the home that does not qualify.

levels.title: The Night Watch
levels.tagline: The alley runs a night shift, and the night shift has rules.

lessons.title: Workers Compensation
lessons.subtitle: A social remedy, the exceptions, and the six policy parts.
lessons.intro: Workers compensation is the clearest place where a social policy sits inside an insurance contract. It trades the employer's old courtroom defenses for a promise of benefits no matter who was at fault.

teaching.heading: A social remedy
teaching.text: Workers compensation exists to answer three defenses an employer once used to escape liability: assumption of risk, contributory negligence, and the fellow servant rule. The system pays an injured worker whether or not anyone was negligent, which is why it is described as a social remedy rather than a fault-based one.

teaching.heading: Who must carry it
teaching.text: Coverage is required for nearly every class of employment, with a short list of exceptions: real estate brokers and salespersons, farm workers, domestic workers and homemakers, employers whose payroll falls below twenty thousand dollars, workers already covered by federal law, and sole proprietors, partners and the self-employed. A company's owners may choose to exclude themselves from the policy. When an employer skips required coverage, three things follow: the worker still receives the benefit the policy would have paid, the employer commits a misdemeanor and is fined, and the worker's benefits are increased as an added penalty.

teaching.heading: Structure and rating
teaching.text: The policy is built from six parts: Part I statutory benefits, Part II employers liability, Part III other state's coverage, Part IV the insured employer's duties when an injury occurs - supplying medical care, reporting the injury and cooperating with the insurer - Part V premiums, and Part VI conditions. Payroll is estimated up front and a deposit premium is collected, then a premium audit at the end of the term settles the final figure. Loss experience over three years drives any adjustment: an experience modification lowers the premium when losses run below average, and a surcharge raises it when they run above. Rates are quoted per one hundred dollars of payroll for each job classification, and a risk the market will not accept may be placed through the Kansas Workers Compensation Insurance Plan.

scenario.title: The night crew at the market
scenario.text: The grocery store keeps a night crew to unload trucks, and one of them goes down on a wet floor at two in the morning. The owner wants three answers: does a worker who was partly careless still collect, must a store with a small payroll carry coverage at all, and what happens if the policy was never bought. CAT watches from the top of a pallet while the fellow servant rule and the deposit premium audit get untangled.

lessons.title: Benefits and the Umbrella
lessons.subtitle: Statutory benefits, exclusive remedy, and broad excess coverage.
lessons.intro: The Kansas act separates workers compensation into statutory benefits and common law employers liability. Above both sits the umbrella, ready to answer what the primary policies leave behind.

teaching.heading: Part One and its benefits
teaching.text: Part One responds to statutory claims an employee brings for occupational injury or occupational disease that grows out of the employment relationship. The benefits include unlimited medical care with mileage paid beyond five miles plus a per diem, a loss of time benefit with a seven-day elimination period and retroactive payment after three weeks, temporary partial and temporary total disability subject to state minimums and a $130,000 maximum, permanent partial disability paid through scheduled injury awards, permanent total disability capped at $155,000, and survivor's death benefits of a $300,000 lump sum with survivor income for a widow and children to age eighteen, or twenty-three while still in school, plus a $5,000 burial allowance. A worker must give notice within ten days of an accident, or within ninety days of an illness diagnosis.

teaching.heading: Part Two and exclusive remedy
teaching.text: Part Two answers common law claims against the employer, including suits by workers outside the Compensation Act and third-party actions against the insured. It carries a basic liability limit of $100,000 that can be raised. It does not cover punitive damages, an injury to a worker employed in violation of the law with the insured's knowledge, intentional injury, injury outside the United States and Canada, damages from discrimination, or obligations already imposed by workers compensation law. Under exclusive remedy, the employer answers for work-related injury and disease no matter who was at fault, and in exchange the injured worker gives up the right to sue over the employer's negligence.

teaching.heading: Umbrella liability
teaching.text: Umbrella liability, also called excess liability, layers broad excess coverage above primary limits and has no standard form. A personal umbrella in the example sits above auto, boat and homeowners limits of $300,000 each, while a commercial umbrella sits above a general liability limit of one million, employers liability of one million, and the business auto limit of one million, using a one million dollar umbrella limit. Where no primary coverage exists at all, the umbrella still responds, but only after a self-insured retention that works like a deductible.

scenario.title: The fall from the loading dock
scenario.text: The night worker from the wet floor now needs surgery, and the numbers start to matter: the seven-day elimination period, the mileage benefit, and the survivor benefits that would have applied had the fall gone worse. A separate suit against the store names a third party, and the owner wants to know whether the umbrella answers above the general liability limit. CAT, who has absorbed plenty of hard landings, listens while the figures and the exclusive remedy rule get sorted out.

lessons.title: Professional Liability and Bonds
lessons.subtitle: E&O, D&O, employment practices, and the three parties to a bond.
lessons.intro: Professional liability answers for advice, judgment and decisions rather than for accidents. Bonds look similar until you check who pays and who is protected, and there are three parties to keep straight.

teaching.heading: Professional liability coverages
teaching.text: Professional liability protects an insured who fails to perform the services they were hired for, or performs them below the appropriate standard of conduct. Errors and omissions covers exposures that grow out of knowledge, skill or advice, and is written for advertisers, broadcasters, publishers, insurance agents, accountants, real estate agents and brokers, architects, engineers, attorneys, pension plan fiduciaries and stockbrokers; the lawyers form automatically covers every member attorney of the firm as a named insured without listing them. Directors and officers coverage defends directors and officers against stockholder suits over wrongful acts and decisions that cost stockholders money, and it protects each of them individually while they carry out their duties. Employment practices liability answers wrongful termination, discrimination, and verbal, physical, mental or emotional abuse of an employee. Medical malpractice is professional liability for health care providers and may include a consent to settle clause that requires the insurer to obtain the insured's consent before settling. Data breach or cyber liability responds when personal information a business collected is leaked or hacked and causes a financial loss to customers.

teaching.heading: The three bond parties
teaching.text: The obligee-insured is the party who collects on the bond when the obligor-principal defaults, and is the party the bond protects. The surety-guarantor is the insurance company, which guarantees the obligee that the obligor-principal will meet its obligations or the surety will pay instead. The obligor-principal is the party who is bonded and whose obligation is being guaranteed; if that party defaults, the surety pays the penalty to the obligee.

teaching.heading: Fidelity and surety
teaching.text: Fidelity bonds shield an employer from loss caused by an employee's dishonest or negligent acts, and coverage for that employee ends once the dishonesty is discovered; a discovery period gives the business owner two years to determine whether a former employee took money or property. Surety bonds are issued by the surety to guarantee that the obligor-principal fulfills an obligation to the obligee-insured, and a surety bond runs only as long as it takes the principal to meet that obligation. Fidelity bonds are arranged and paid for by the obligee-insured, while surety bonds are arranged and paid for by the obligor-principal.

scenario.title: The bonding of the small shop
scenario.text: A contractor who owes the market money must post a bond before it can start repairing the loading dock, and the owner wants to know who is protected if the contractor simply walks away. The same week, the store's bookkeeper is caught lifting cash from the register, and the owner asks how the fidelity bond responds and how long there is to discover the loss. CAT settles onto the counter while the paperwork sorts out the obligee, the obligor and the surety.

levels.title: The Highway Verge
levels.tagline: The fastest way out of the alley is also the loudest.

lessons.title: Personal Auto: Cards on the Table
lessons.subtitle: Which vehicles count, how a fresh purchase is covered, and who else may drive.
lessons.intro: Every auto claim begins with definitions, not dollars. Before anyone talks about limits, the policy has already decided whether this vehicle is a covered auto, how long a car bought last week stays protected, and whose hands were allowed on the wheel.

teaching.heading: Naming the coverages
teaching.text: Bodily injury liability answers for harm the insured causes to other people with the car, including sickness, disease and death. Property damage liability answers for the other party's vehicle or any other property of theirs that the car strikes. Physical damage is the part that repairs the insured's own car, split into collision and other than collision, the second of which is also called comprehensive.

teaching.heading: Covered autos and newly acquired vehicles
teaching.text: A covered auto is any vehicle listed on the declarations page, plus private passenger autos and pick-ups or vans under ten thousand pounds with four wheels or more, along with trailers the insured owns, whose liability rides along automatically whether attached or being towed. A car added to the household gets fourteen days of automatic protection for every coverage the insured already carries, but just four days of collision and other than collision coverage when no existing vehicle has that coverage, and a five hundred dollar deductible applies. A car that replaces another inherits the coverage of the vehicle it replaced, leaving four days to add it or fourteen days to continue Coverage D, while liability keeps running to the end of the policy term with no notice needed. A temporary substitute is whatever the insured drives while the usual car is being repaired, and a vehicle leased for more than six months is treated as if owned.

teaching.heading: Insured persons and territory
teaching.text: Other insured persons include anyone driving the insured car with assumed permission and family members, meaning resident relatives such as a ward or foster child. The named insured also takes in the spouse while the couple lives together and for ninety days following a separation or divorce. Exclusions reach intentional acts, damage to property being hauled, prearranged racing, and non-owned autos furnished for the insured's regular use. The policy territory is the United States, its territories and possessions, Puerto Rico and Canada, with nothing at all in Mexico.

scenario.title: The borrowed truck and the new car
scenario.text: A neighbor takes the market's delivery truck for an afternoon, and the owner signs for a second car the same week. A wheel shears off the borrowed truck at a stoplight. CAT, who only ever crosses roads after dark, listens while the owner works through two questions: whose insurance stands behind the borrowed truck, and how many mornings of automatic collision coverage the new car actually has.

lessons.title: Auto Coverages and Kansas Law
lessons.subtitle: Liability, PIP, uninsured motorist, physical damage, and the reparations act.
lessons.intro: Kansas law writes part of the personal auto policy for you. Required limits, mandatory personal injury protection, and the narrow doorway through which an injured person may sue for non-pecuniary harm all come from the state, not the form.

teaching.heading: Liability and supplementary payments
teaching.text: Liability coverage is mandatory, and Kansas sets split limits of twenty-five thousand per person and fifty thousand per occurrence for bodily injury, with twenty-five thousand for property damage, written 25/50/25. Supplementary payments sit on top of those limits and take in investigation and defense costs, a two hundred fifty dollar premium on bail bonds, appeal bond premiums, interest that accrues after judgment, two hundred dollars a day for lost earnings while attending trials or hearings at the company's request, and other reasonable expenses incurred at the company's request.

teaching.heading: Personal injury protection
teaching.text: Personal injury protection is no fault coverage. It provides forty-five hundred dollars for medical bills, forty-five hundred dollars for rehabilitation, one hundred percent of income up to nine hundred dollars a month for as long as twelve months, a nine hundred dollar monthly survivor benefit for up to twelve months for a spouse and children under eighteen, two thousand dollars for funeral expenses, and twenty-five dollars a day for essential services, with a floor of three hundred sixty-five days. PIP pays the insured, family members, and people riding in the insured's car who do not own a car of their own; a family member or other passenger who does own a car cannot collect from the insured's PIP. Occupying means in, upon, in the act of getting in or out, near, under or around the car.

teaching.heading: Uninsured motorist, physical damage and the Kansas act
teaching.text: Uninsured motorist pays the insured's own injuries when hit by a car with no insurance, a car whose insurer has been declared insolvent, or a hit and run car, while underinsured motorist makes up the difference between the other driver's limits and the insured's own; the other driver must be at fault, and the uninsured and underinsured limits have to match. Physical damage pays actual cash value, carries a deductible, and answers for collision or other than collision, with collisions involving animals, theft, earthquake and flood falling under other than collision. Under Kansas law a person may not sue another party for non-pecuniary injuries unless the threshold is crossed: more than two thousand dollars in medical bills, damage to a weight bearing bone, or permanent disfigurement or disability.

scenario.title: Two cars and a broken wrist
scenario.text: A driver carrying no insurance blows through a light at the highway verge and strikes a market employee's car. The employee holds PIP and uninsured motorist coverage and leaves with a broken wrist. CAT watches from the far side of the fence as the family asks whether PIP picks up the medical bills, whether uninsured motorist responds, and whether pain and suffering can be claimed when the bills only reach fifteen hundred dollars.

lessons.title: Business Auto, Garage and Boats
lessons.subtitle: Nine symbols, garage liability, and a policy that floats.
lessons.intro: The business auto policy swaps the personal form's single covered auto idea for nine numbered symbols. Garage and watercraft coverage then carry the same reasoning over to vehicles a business holds for customers and to a boat that never touches a road.

teaching.heading: The nine coverage symbols
teaching.text: Section I of the business auto policy covers vehicles through nine symbols: one, any auto, the broadest; two, owned autos only; three, owned private passenger autos only; four, owned autos other than private passenger autos; five, owned autos subject to no fault benefits, required in Kansas; six, owned autos subject to the compulsory uninsured motorists law, also required in Kansas; seven, specifically described autos only, the narrowest; eight, hired autos only; and nine, non-owned autos only. A newly acquired auto is covered automatically to the end of the policy term under symbols one through six, but under symbol seven it gets only thirty days.

teaching.heading: Business auto liability and conditions
teaching.text: Business auto liability is written in Kansas at 25/50/25 or a minimum single limit of seventy-five thousand dollars, built as a single limit policy that may be endorsed to split limits, and it carries the customary defense and supplementary payments. Insured persons are the named insured for any covered auto; the owner or anyone else from whom a trailer is hired or borrowed and connected to an auto the named insured owns; anyone using with permission a covered auto owned, hired or borrowed by the named insured; and anyone liable for an insured's conduct, but only up to that liability. Physical damage options are collision and upset, comprehensive, specified causes of loss, towing with a basic limit of twenty-five dollars, and extensions for transportation expenses of twenty dollars a day up to six hundred dollars, starting forty-eight hours after a theft. Auto means a land motor vehicle, trailer or semi-trailer built for public roads, though mobile equipment is covered while carried or towed by a covered auto for liability only, and cleanup of pollutants being carried by a vehicle and not used in its operation is not covered.

teaching.heading: Garage and watercraft
teaching.text: Garagekeepers is optional bailee coverage for damage to vehicles left in a business's custody for repair or service, and it can answer for collision and other than collision to a customer's vehicle on either a primary or excess basis over the customer's own coverage. Garage liability is required: the dealers form serves businesses that sell autos and covers owned and non-owned autos on a primary basis, while the service form serves service stations, repair shops and parking garages and covers non-owned autos on a primary basis. Boatowners or watercraft coverage mirrors auto insurance, with liability for bodily injury and property damage to others plus the same supplementary payments, medical payments for the insured and others hurt while boating, and physical damage for collision and other than collision after deductibles on the boat, motors, trailer, attached equipment and miscellaneous equipment. Lay-up warranties are common where winters bite.

scenario.title: The lot, the lift, and the lake
scenario.text: The market's owner opens a small repair bay, rolls a customer's car onto the lift, and buys a used boat for weekend runs to the lake. A customer's car is scratched on the lift, and hail dents the boat. CAT, unimpressed by vehicles of any size, listens while the agent explains which business auto symbol fits a borrowed car, whether garagekeepers pays before or after the customer's own policy, and why a lay-up warranty belongs on a boat.

levels.title: The Long Shadow
levels.tagline: Everything the alley taught, and the shape waiting at the end of it.

lessons.title: The Businessowners Policy
lessons.subtitle: Who can buy it, what it pays, and the single property form behind it.
lessons.intro: The businessowners policy is the small-commercial workhorse. It is a packaged product with a short eligibility list, firm size ceilings, and one open peril property form doing most of the work.

teaching.heading: Who may buy the form
teaching.text: The businessowners policy is a packaged commercial contract with very few optional pieces. It is aimed at certain small and medium sized firms and carries a single property form written on an open peril, all risk basis. Size ceilings are strict: no building over six stories, no more than one hundred thousand square feet of total floor area, a maximum of twenty-five thousand square feet for any one occupant, and gross receipts no higher than three million dollars. Apartments, offices, retail shops, some processing and service operations, and residential or office condominiums all fit the program. Bars, grills and restaurants, condominium associations outside the office and residential classes, contractors, amusement operations such as carnivals, bowling alleys and theatres, wholesalers, financial institutions, and auto dealers or auto repair shops do not.

teaching.heading: Section I property coverages
teaching.text: Buildings and business personal property settle at replacement cost, and the building limit carries an automatic percentage increase, often called inflation guard, set on the declarations page. Peak season coverage adds a twenty-five percent automatic bump during busy periods at no extra premium. Business income is written as an unlimited dollar amount that runs to the expected date of business resumption but never past twelve months. Outdoor signs are insured up to one thousand dollars, and bailee's customer coverage protects property customers leave with the business. Optional pieces include employee dishonesty, which is a fidelity bond, boiler and pressure vessel or mechanical breakdown, burglary robbery and theft, money and securities, and additional outdoor signage. If a building stays vacant beyond sixty days, theft, vandalism and sprinkler leakage are dropped entirely and every other loss is trimmed by fifteen percent.

teaching.heading: Section II liability and the money words
teaching.text: Section II packages premises and operations, personal injury, advertising injury, products and completed operations, fire legal liability at three hundred thousand dollars per occurrence for lawsuit protection, and medical payments to others paid without regard to fault. Business income pays the salaries, payroll and continuing expenses a business keeps paying during a shutdown caused by a covered peril; the period of restoration generally begins after a direct covered loss and ends when the building is repaired, replaced or rebuilt. Extra expense reimburses costs a business takes on when it temporarily moves so it does not lose income. A reporting form suits inventory that swings, letting the insured report values on a regular schedule, and the honesty clause punishes under-reporting by cutting the loss payment by that same percentage. Supplemental payments cover defense, investigation and claim costs and are paid on top of the limit of liability.

scenario.title: The grill that would not fit
scenario.text: The market owner wants to open a small grill beside the store and asks whether one businessowners policy can cover the retail operation and the new restaurant. CAT, who has strong opinions about restaurants, listens while the agent walks through the ineligible list, the twenty-five thousand square foot ceiling for a single occupant, and what happens to coverage when a building sits empty past sixty days. Then the owner asks how a reporting form treats inventory that surges before the holidays.

lessons.title: General Liability in Depth
lessons.subtitle: The offense coverages, the products problem, and the claims made trigger.
lessons.intro: The commercial general liability form is assembled from distinct pieces, each with its own logic. The claims made form then decides when a claim must arrive, and the conditions govern everything else.

teaching.heading: The building blocks
teaching.text: Premises and operations responds to bodily injury or property damage that happens at the business or grows out of the work the business does. Advertising injury and personal injury are offense coverages and never pay for bodily injury or property damage: advertising injury reaches defamation committed while advertising a product, including misappropriation of advertising ideas or style and infringement of title or slogan, while personal injury adds wrongful entry or eviction and false arrest, detention, imprisonment and malicious prosecution. Fire legal, sometimes called tenant liability, covers damage an insured causes to the leased or rented portion of a building by fire or explosion, with the rest of the building left to premises liability. Medical payments to others pays the medical bills of other people whether or not the insured was negligent, up to one year from the occurrence, in order to head off lawsuits.

teaching.heading: Products, completed work and employees
teaching.text: Product liability answers for bodily injury or property damage a defective product causes, but never for damage to the product itself or the cost of recalling it, and such suits are usually settled under strict liability. The harm must happen away from the business premises, except for restaurants, and the product must be entirely in the customer's control. Completed operations picks up defective workmanship or design that causes injury or damage later, once the insured has finished the job and left the site; it is always an off-premises exposure. Injuries to employees belong to workers compensation, while injuries that employees cause to non-employees are handled by the commercial general liability form.

teaching.heading: The claims made form and reporting windows
teaching.text: Commercial general liability comes in two flavors. On an occurrence form the occurrence must fall inside the policy period while the claim may surface at any time afterward. On a claims made form both the occurrence and the claim must fall inside the policy period. A retroactive date caps how far back coverage reaches for occurrences that predate the policy. The basic extended reporting period comes automatically at no charge: sixty days after the policy ends for any claim, and if the insured reports occurrences that happened during the policy period inside those sixty days, a five-year window opens for claims arising from those reported occurrences only. The supplemental extended reporting period is optional and purchased, and it adds an unlimited extension for claims from occurrences that happened during the policy period, beginning when the basic window closes.

scenario.title: The jar and the roof
scenario.text: A shopper takes home a jar of the store's own chili, eats it, and falls ill; the jar was made and sold on site and stayed in the customer's hands after that. In the same week a tenant complains that water poured through her ceiling while the store's crew worked on the roof above her shop. CAT, who has eaten worse, listens as the adjuster pulls products apart from completed operations and premises apart from the roof work, then asks whether the tenant's claim arrived soon enough to matter under a claims made form.

lessons.title: The Shadow at the Edge
lessons.subtitle: The commercial package, property on the move, and the language of crime.
lessons.intro: The last lesson assembles the commercial package, the coverage that follows property as it travels, and the crime form whose definitions turn on whether anyone was present and whether there was evidence of force.

teaching.heading: The commercial package
teaching.text: The commercial package policy is a customizable product, not a package in the businessowners sense, and it is built for larger operations. Its common policy declarations name the company and the insureds, note that the first name listed carries the first named insured duties, and record the policy period, described premises, mortgage holder, description of business, each coverage part's premium, and the list of forms. Coverage parts include commercial property, commercial inland marine, commercial general liability and commercial crime. Common policy conditions cover cancellation, changes, premiums, examination of books and records, inspections and surveys, assignment, and the first named insured, who may cancel, make changes, and receives both the bill and any premium refund.

teaching.heading: Inland marine
teaching.text: Inland marine insures certain kinds of property and is almost always written on a special form. It excludes war, nuclear events, wear and tear, deterioration, inherent vice, and insects or vermin. State law keeps inland marine forms inside three categories of property, and neither real property nor a building's contents may be insured on inland marine paper. Business personal property stops being covered once it sits more than one hundred feet from the premises, truck or not. Available classes include accounts receivable, commercial articles, contractor equipment floaters, electronic data processing, installation floaters, signs, valuable papers and records, and bailee's customer coverage for items in the business's care, custody and control. A floater covers property that moves from place to place, and inherent vice is the process by which property destroys itself over time, like rust eating metal. Personal inland marine lines include article floaters for guns, jewelry and furs.

teaching.heading: Commercial crime
teaching.text: Burglary is the taking of property with visible evidence of forced entry into or out of a premises or safe, after hours, with no people present. Robbery is the taking of property by causing or threatening bodily harm during hours when people are present. Theft is any act of stealing and is the broadest crime coverage. Extortion is handing over property away from the premises because of a threat to harm the insured, an employee, or a captive relative, and pilferage is stealing in small amounts. A custodian is the insured, a relative, a partner or member, or an employee who has care and custody of property inside the premises, but never a watchperson or janitor; a messenger holds care and custody outside the premises. Mysterious disappearance means property is gone with no evidence a crime took place. Employee dishonesty, the fidelity bond, covers dishonest acts by employees, ends coverage for an employee once a dishonest act is discovered, and gives the owner a discovery period of two years to find out whether a former employee took money or property.

scenario.title: The night the dock door opened
scenario.text: Someone pries open the loading dock door, removes two crates, and nobody notices until morning. That same week a courier is threatened at the curb and surrenders a deposit bag, and a sheaf of invoices vanishes from a desk with no sign of a break-in at all. CAT, who has watched every kind of night, listens while the owner sorts burglary from robbery from mysterious disappearance, and asks whether the dry cleaner's customer's coat still counts as covered property.

boss.title: The Shadow at the End of Level Nine
boss.intro: Nine levels are behind CAT, and the red car is idling at the edge of town. Between them stands the last challenger: SHADOW CAT, her own shadow - everything survival taught her, turned around and looking back.
boss.dialogue: You learned the rules to survive the alley. Now show me you can use them when nothing is chasing you and no clock is playing tricks.
boss.win: SHADOW CAT steps aside. It was never an enemy, only the part of CAT that had nowhere to go. And down the road the red car is waiting, with the mother who will bring her home.
boss.lose: SHADOW CAT holds its ground. Not a defeat, only another round: the rules are still there to be learned, and the red car will still be waiting next time.
